produced_by: claude-fable-5-1 labellers working in parallel from reference/labelling-brief.txt, each shown the review text alone
notes: Helldivers 2. Labelled from snapshot=1788883156, which holds 1,161,047 of the 1,161,166 reviews Valve reports (99.99%), across 38 date shards. Three shards stalled mid-window and were re-walked before the capture was accepted.

Drawn by `census sample 296970 3551340 548430 275850 1091500 553850 --out data --random 100 --per-category 40 --seed 1 --brief --batch-size 35`. The stratified subset is pooled across all six games, so a category one game barely discusses is supplied by a game that does. The same seed against the same capture draws the same reviews, which is why sample.json need not be kept.

247 labels: 147 stratified and 100 random. The two subsets have different jobs and must not be merged. The stratified labels are TRAINING DATA, so any figure measured over them says what the anchors memorised. The random labels are held back from fitting entirely and are the only ones that measure anything.

Labellers were given the review text and the category sheet, never the classifier's prediction. Agreement measured against this set is therefore not inflated by labellers anchoring on the guess they are being compared against.

67 of the 247 labels (27.1%) are flagged ambiguous because the labeller said the call was genuinely contested. Disagreement on those says as much about the taxonomy as about the classifier, which is why `census evaluate` reports them apart.

The largest corpus of the six and the one that carries `policy`. Its review-bombing over a required second account produced tens of thousands of reviews that name a requirement rather than the game, which is the case that forced `policy` and its boundary rule into the spine. It also carries the balance-patch argument, where `updates` and `difficulty` compete for the same sentence.

Measured with anchors pooled from all six sets: 56.0% primary agreement on the held-out random subset [46.2, 65.3], macro F1 0.381. Split by how the labeller called it, 71.2% on the 73 clear-cut reviews and 14.8% on the 27 contested ones, the widest gap of the six. `policy` reaches precision 0.93 at recall 0.48: when the classifier calls a review a policy complaint it is almost always right, and it misses half of them.

Anchors fitted on the other five games and never on this one reach 46.0% against 16.0% for the written descriptions: 37 reviews move to the right category and 7 move away. The descriptions are at their worst on this game of the six, which is what a corpus of short protest reviews should be expected to do to prose written about topics.

Pooled over all six held-out random subsets, 600 reviews in total: written descriptions agree with the labels on 30.0%, anchors fitted on the five other games on 46.3%, and anchors fitted on all six on 52.7%. Of the 242 reviews the descriptions and the unseen-game fit place differently, 170 move to the category the labels give and 72 move away (exact McNemar p < 0.0001). Labels from other games are therefore worth about 16 points, and labelling the game itself a further 6. Split by how the labeller called it, the pooled figure is 62.1% on the 435 clear-cut reviews and 27.9% on the 165 contested ones. Reproduce with `census fit 296970 3551340 548430 275850 1091500 553850 --out data --leave-one-out`.

Because no person has checked these labels, results measured against this set are AGREEMENT WITH A MODEL and must never be reported as accuracy. Two language models agreeing can be wrong together, and the sarcasm and boundary cases where this classifier is weakest are exactly where that correlation is strongest. Set human_verified to true only once a person has labelled a subset independently, and record how large that subset was.

Taxonomy gaps the labellers reported, worth weighing before any future spine: tutorial and onboarding quality, asked for by three separate labellers and currently split between gameplay and difficulty; co-op as a genre trait rather than a multiplayer feature; real-world licensing with no home of its own; VR support and immersion; and protests that name a publisher but no requirement, which the offtopic boundary sends to offtopic and which this game produces in bulk.
